title: Physical: Solar Radiation, Heat Balance and Temperature

learn.hook: Here's a surprise: the earth is closest to the sun in January, yet that is when Delhi shivers in winter.
points: The energy received by the earth from the sun is called incoming solar radiation, or insolation. The earth's surface receives most of it in short wavelengths.
Because the earth is a geoid resembling a sphere, the sun's rays fall obliquely at the top of the atmosphere, and the earth intercepts only a very small portion of the sun's energy.
On average, the earth receives 1.94 calories per sq cm per minute at the top of its atmosphere.

On 4 July the earth is farthest from the sun (152 million km): aphelion. On 3 January it is nearest (147 million km): perihelion. So annual insolation received on 3 January is slightly more than on 4 July.
This variation is masked by other factors such as the distribution of land and sea and atmospheric circulation, so it has no great effect on daily weather.

example.q: How much closer to the sun is the earth at perihelion than at aphelion?
steps: Aphelion distance = 152 million km.
Perihelion distance = 147 million km.
Difference = 152 − 147 = 5 million km.
example.answer: 5 million km closer at perihelion (3 January).

learn.reallife: ISRO's Aditya-L1 solar observatory measures the sun's output from space, above the atmosphere, where insolation is not reduced by clouds or dust.

topics.title: Why insolation varies: axis, angle and day length

learn.hook: Shine a torch straight down and you get a small bright circle; tilt it and the light spreads into a dim oval. That is why the poles are cold.
points: The amount and intensity of insolation vary during a day, a season and a year. The factors are: (i) rotation of the earth on its axis, (ii) angle of inclination of the sun's rays, (iii) length of the day, (iv) transparency of the atmosphere, (v) configuration of land in terms of its aspect. The last two have less influence.
The earth's axis makes an angle of 66½° with the plane of its orbit around the sun. This greatly influences the insolation received at different latitudes.
The angle of the sun's rays depends on latitude. The higher the latitude, the smaller the angle the rays make with the surface, giving slant rays.
Slant rays spread over a larger area than vertical rays, so energy per unit area falls. They also pass through a greater depth of atmosphere, causing more absorption, scattering and diffusion.

example.q: The earth's axis makes 66½° with the plane of its orbit. What angle does it make with the perpendicular to that plane?
steps: The perpendicular makes 90° with the plane.
Tilt from the perpendicular = 90° − 66½°.

learn.reallife: Solar panels in Ladakh are tilted at a steeper angle than those in Tamil Nadu so that the sun's rays strike them more directly.

topics.title: Insolation through the atmosphere and its distribution

learn.hook: Why is the sky blue at noon and the sun red at sunset? Blame scattering by tiny particles in the air.
points: The atmosphere is largely transparent to short-wave solar radiation. In the troposphere, water vapour, ozone and other gases absorb much of the near-infrared radiation.

Very small suspended particles in the troposphere scatter the visible spectrum both to space and towards the surface. The blue colour of the sky and the red colour of the rising and setting sun are results of scattering.
Insolation at the surface varies from about 320 W/m² in the tropics to about 70 W/m² at the poles.
Maximum insolation is received over the subtropical deserts, where cloudiness is least. The equator receives comparatively less insolation than the tropics.
At the same latitude, insolation is generally more over continents than over oceans. In winter, middle and higher latitudes receive less radiation than in summer.

example.q: Why do subtropical deserts receive more insolation than the equator, even though the sun is higher over the equator?
steps: Insolation reaching the surface depends on cloudiness as well as sun angle.
The equator has thick clouds and heavy rain, which reflect and absorb insolation.
Subtropical deserts have the least cloudiness.
So more insolation reaches the surface in subtropical deserts.
example.answer: Because subtropical deserts have the least cloud cover, while the equator is very cloudy.

learn.reallife: Rajasthan's Bhadla Solar Park sits in the dry subtropics, where clear skies give some of the highest solar energy in India.

topics.title: Heating the atmosphere: conduction, convection and advection

learn.hook: In May, a scorching wind called the loo sweeps across north India and can push temperatures past 45°C. It is heat delivered sideways by advection.
points: The earth, heated by insolation, transmits heat to the layers of the atmosphere near it in long-wave form.

Conduction: when two bodies of unequal temperature are in contact, energy flows from the warmer to the cooler body until both reach the same temperature or contact is broken. Air in contact with land gets heated, and the layers above get heated by contact. Conduction is important in heating the lower layers of the atmosphere.
Convection: heated air near the surface rises vertically in currents and transmits heat upward. This vertical heating is convection; it is confined to the troposphere.

Advection: transfer of heat through horizontal movement of air. Horizontal movement is relatively more important than vertical movement. In middle latitudes, most diurnal variation in daily weather is caused by advection alone.
In tropical regions, especially northern India in summer, the local wind called 'loo' is the outcome of advection.

example.q: Name the heat-transfer process: (a) a warm road heating the air just above it; (b) a column of hot air rising over farmland on a summer afternoon; (c) hot loo winds blowing across Uttar Pradesh.
steps: (a) Heat passing to air in contact with the surface → conduction.
(b) Heated air rising vertically → convection.
(c) Heat carried horizontally by wind → advection.

learn.reallife: IMD issues heatwave alerts when loo winds carry desert heat across Rajasthan, Haryana and Uttar Pradesh in May and June.

topics.title: Terrestrial radiation, Planck's law and specific heat

learn.hook: The sun heats the ground, and the ground heats the air. That's why it's cooler on a mountain top even though it's closer to the sun.
points: Insolation in short waves heats the earth's surface. The heated earth becomes a radiating body and radiates energy to the atmosphere in long-wave form. This is terrestrial radiation; it heats the atmosphere from below.
Long-wave radiation is absorbed by atmospheric gases, particularly carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases. So the atmosphere is indirectly heated by the earth's radiation.

The atmosphere in turn radiates and transmits heat to space. The heat received from the sun is finally returned to space, maintaining a constant temperature at the surface and in the atmosphere over time.
Planck's law: the hotter a body, the more energy it radiates and the shorter the wavelength of that radiation. That is why the very hot sun emits short waves and the cooler earth emits long waves.
Specific heat is the energy needed to raise the temperature of one gram of a substance by one degree Celsius.

example.q: Use Planck's law to explain why the sun emits short waves and the earth emits long waves.
steps: Planck's law: hotter bodies radiate more energy at shorter wavelengths.
The sun is extremely hot, so its radiation is short-wave.
The earth is much cooler, so it radiates long-wave (terrestrial) radiation.
example.answer: The sun is much hotter, so it radiates at shorter wavelengths; the cooler earth radiates long waves.

learn.reallife: Thermal cameras used by firefighters and in airport fever screening detect the long-wave radiation that warm bodies give off.

teach.nudge: Explain terrestrial radiation, how the air is heated, and Planck's law.

remember: Terrestrial radiation = long waves; heats atmosphere from below
Planck's law: hotter body → more energy, shorter wavelength

topics.title: Heat budget I: reflection, albedo and absorption

learn.hook: Imagine the sun pays the earth 100 rupees of energy every day. Where does every rupee go? The heat budget is that account book.
points: The earth as a whole does not accumulate or lose heat; it maintains its temperature. This happens because the insolation received is balanced by the radiation sent back to space.

Take insolation at the top of the atmosphere as 100 units. About 35 units are sent back to space before reaching the surface: 27 units reflected from the tops of clouds, 2 units reflected from snow and ice-covered areas, and 6 units scattered to space.
The reflected amount of radiation is called the albedo of the earth.
The remaining 65 units are absorbed: 14 units within the atmosphere and 51 units by the earth's surface.

example.q: Check that the units add up: 35 units lost before reaching the surface and 65 absorbed.
steps: Lost: 27 (clouds) + 2 (snow and ice) + 6 (scattered) = 35.
Absorbed: 14 (atmosphere) + 51 (surface) = 65.
Total: 35 + 65 = 100 units.
example.answer: 35 + 65 = 100 units, so all incoming insolation is accounted for.

learn.reallife: Melting Himalayan snow lowers the region's albedo, so the ground absorbs more heat and warms faster, a worrying feedback watched by Indian climate scientists.

Answer: 51

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Where does all the sunshine energy go after it reaches the earth?'

remember: Albedo 35 = 27 clouds + 2 snow/ice + 6 scattered
Absorbed 65 = 14 atmosphere + 51 surface
traps: Don't confuse the 14 units (atmosphere) with 51 (surface)
Albedo is reflected radiation, not absorbed radiation

topics.title: Heat budget II: terrestrial radiation and the balance

learn.hook: The ground absorbs 51 units. It gives them all back, but not all in the same way. Some go straight to space, some warm the air, and some ride up with evaporated water.
points: The earth radiates back the 51 units it absorbed, as terrestrial radiation.

Of these, 17 units are radiated directly to space. The remaining 34 units are absorbed by the atmosphere: 6 units absorbed directly, 9 units through convection and turbulence, and 19 units through latent heat of condensation.
The atmosphere absorbs 48 units in total (14 from insolation + 34 from terrestrial radiation) and radiates them back into space.
Total radiation returning to space from the earth and the atmosphere = 17 + 48 = 65 units, which balances the 65 units absorbed from the sun. This is the heat budget or heat balance of the earth.
NCERT's flow diagram shows these units moving between space, the atmosphere and the earth's surface.

example.q: Show that the heat budget balances.
steps: Absorbed from the sun: 14 (atmosphere) + 51 (surface) = 65 units.
Surface gives back 51: 17 directly to space + 34 to the atmosphere (6 + 9 + 19).
Atmosphere radiates 14 + 34 = 48 units to space.
Returned to space: 17 + 48 = 65 units = absorbed.
example.answer: 65 units in = 65 units out, so the earth's heat budget balances.

learn.reallife: Monsoon clouds over India release enormous latent heat when vapour condenses into rain, part of the 19 units in the heat budget.

A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

steps: A: latent heat of condensation is the largest single route of heat to the atmosphere. True.
R: it gives 19 of the 34 units. True.
19 is more than 9 or 6, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How does the earth give back the heat it gets? Does it balance?'

teach.nudge: Explain how the 51 units are returned and why the total balances at 65.

topics.title: Variation in the net heat budget

learn.hook: The tropics get more energy than they lose, and the poles lose more than they get. Without a heat delivery service, the tropics would bake and the poles would freeze solid.
points: The heat budget balances for the whole earth, but not for every latitude.
There is a surplus of net radiation between 40°N and 40°S, and the regions near the poles have a deficit.
The surplus heat from the tropics is redistributed polewards by winds and ocean currents.
As a result, the tropics do not get progressively hotter from accumulating excess heat, and the high latitudes do not get permanently frozen.
NCERT shows this as a graph of net radiation against latitude: positive (surplus) in low latitudes, negative (deficit) towards the poles.

example.q: Kolkata (about 22°N) and a station in Norway (about 70°N): which has a net radiation surplus and which a deficit?
steps: Surplus zone: between 40°N and 40°S.
22°N lies within it → surplus.
70°N lies poleward of 40°N → deficit.
example.answer: Kolkata: surplus; the Norwegian station: deficit.

learn.reallife: Warm ocean currents like the North Atlantic Drift carry tropical heat to north-west Europe, keeping its ports ice-free, an example of heat redistribution.

topics.title: Temperature and the factors controlling it

learn.hook: Mumbai and Nagpur are at almost the same latitude, but Nagpur roasts in May while Mumbai stays milder. Distance from the sea explains a lot.
points: Heat represents the molecular movement of particles in a substance; temperature is the measurement in degrees of how hot or cold a thing or place is.
Factors controlling temperature distribution: (i) latitude, (ii) altitude, (iii) distance from the sea, (iv) air-mass circulation, (v) warm and cold ocean currents, and local aspects.

Latitude: temperature depends on insolation, which varies with latitude. Altitude: the atmosphere is heated from below, so places near sea level are warmer; temperature generally falls with height at the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 m.

Distance from the sea: the sea heats and cools slowly; land heats and cools quickly. Places near the sea come under the moderating influence of sea and land breezes, so their temperature range is smaller.
Air masses and ocean currents: places under warm air masses are warmer, those under cold air masses colder. Coasts with warm ocean currents are warmer than coasts with cold currents.

example.q: The temperature at sea level is 30°C. Using the normal lapse rate of 6.5°C per 1,000 m, what is the temperature at 2,000 m?
steps: Temperature = 30 − 13 = 17°C.

learn.reallife: Chennai's summer range is smaller than Delhi's partly because sea breezes moderate the coast, while inland Delhi feels the full effect of continentality.

quiz.explain: Temperature falls by about 6.5°C for every 1,000 m rise.

Answer: 6.5°C per 1,000 m

Answer: The molecular movement of particles, while temperature measures how hot or cold something is

quiz.mistake: Thinks distance from the sun is the reason

steps: Warm ocean currents raise coastal temperatures.

Assertion (A): Inland places have a larger range of temperature than coastal places at the same latitude.
Reason (R): Land heats up and cools down more quickly than water.

Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

steps: A: inland places have a larger temperature range than coastal ones. True.
R: land heats and cools faster than water. True.
That rapid heating and cooling is why inland ranges are large, so R explains A.

topics.title: Distribution of temperature: January and July isotherms

learn.hook: Draw lines joining places with equal temperature on a world map and they bend in curious ways, revealing hidden warm currents and frozen continents.
points: Isotherms are lines joining places having equal temperature. They are generally parallel to latitudes, showing the effect of latitude; deviations are more pronounced in January than in July, especially in the Northern Hemisphere.

In January (Northern Hemisphere winter), isotherms deviate to the north over the ocean and to the south over the continent. Warm currents, the Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift, make the North Atlantic warmer so isotherms bend north; over Europe and especially the Siberian plain, temperatures fall sharply and isotherms bend south.
January means: over 27°C in equatorial oceans, over 24°C in the tropics, 2°C to 0°C in middle latitudes, and −18°C to −48°C in the Eurasian continental interior.
In the Southern Hemisphere, larger oceans make isotherms more regular and roughly parallel to latitudes; the 20°C, 10°C and 0°C isotherms run along about 35°S, 45°S and 60°S in January.

In July, isotherms generally run parallel to latitudes. Equatorial oceans exceed 27°C; over 30°C is found over subtropical continental Asia along 30°N. The highest annual range of temperature, more than 60°C, is over north-eastern Eurasia, due to continentality; the least range, 3°C, is between 20°S and 15°N.

example.q: On a January map, isotherms over the North Atlantic bend sharply northwards. What does this tell you?
steps: A northward bend means warm temperatures extend to higher latitudes over that area.
In the North Atlantic, the warm Gulf Stream and North Atlantic Drift flow north-east.
So the ocean there is warmer than other areas at the same latitude in January.
example.answer: Warm ocean currents (Gulf Stream, North Atlantic Drift) are warming the North Atlantic.

learn.reallife: In January, Srinagar can be below freezing while Thiruvananthapuram stays warm, a gradient you could draw with isotherms across India.

topics.title: Inversion of temperature and air drainage

learn.hook: On winter mornings in Delhi, smog and fog hug the ground and flights get delayed. Above that grey blanket, the air is actually warmer.
points: Normally temperature decreases with height (normal lapse rate). When this is reversed and temperature increases with height, it is called inversion of temperature. Inversions are usually short but quite common; over polar areas, inversion is normal throughout the year.
Ideal conditions: a long winter night with clear skies and still air. The day's heat is radiated off at night, so by early morning the earth is cooler than the air above.

Surface inversion promotes stability in the lower atmosphere. Smoke and dust collect beneath the inversion layer and spread horizontally; dense morning fogs are common, especially in winter. The inversion usually lasts a few hours until the sun warms the earth.

Air drainage: in hills and mountains, cold, dense air formed at night flows downslope under gravity, like water, and piles up in pockets and valley bottoms with warm air above. This is why valley floors get frost while slopes are warmer; it protects plants on the slopes from frost damage.
Exam tip: be ready to explain the heat budget, factors controlling temperature, why subtropics get more insolation than the equator, isotherm patterns and conditions for inversion.

example.q: A farmer in a hill valley plants his orchard on the mid-slope instead of the valley floor. Why is this wise?
steps: On clear, calm nights, cold dense air drains down the slopes.
It collects in the valley bottom, causing frost there.
The mid-slopes stay relatively warmer (inversion).
So orchards on slopes are protected from frost damage.
example.answer: Because air drainage collects frost-forming cold air in the valley floor, while slopes stay warmer.

learn.reallife: Apple orchards in Himachal and tea gardens in Darjeeling are often on slopes rather than valley floors, partly to avoid frost pockets created by air drainage.

quiz.q: Inversion of temperature means:
options: Temperature stays the same at all heights
quiz.explain: In an inversion the normal decrease with height is reversed.
steps: Normally temperature falls with height.
In an inversion it is reversed: temperature increases with height.
Answer: Temperature increases with height

quiz.q: The ideal condition for temperature inversion is:
options: A cloudy summer day with strong winds
A long winter night with clear skies and still air
quiz.explain: Clear, calm, long nights let the ground lose heat fast, cooling the air near it.
steps: The ground must lose heat fast to cool the air near it.
This happens on a long winter night with clear skies and still air.
Answer: A long winter night with clear skies and still air

quiz.q: Over which region is temperature inversion normal throughout the year?
quiz.explain: The cold polar surface keeps the lowest air cooler than the air above.
steps: The polar surface stays very cold all year.
So the lowest air is cooler than the air above: inversion is normal there.
Answer: Polar areas

quiz.q: Surface inversion promotes:
options: Stability in the lower layers of the atmosphere
quiz.explain: Cold air below warm air resists rising, so the air is stable.
steps: In a surface inversion cold, dense air lies below warm air.
Such air resists rising, so the lower atmosphere is stable.
Answer: Stability in the lower layers of the atmosphere

quiz.q: Dense fogs on winter mornings are linked with:
quiz.explain: Under inversion, cool air and moisture near the ground produce fog, and smoke and dust collect too.
steps: Under inversion cool, moist air stays near the ground.
This produces dense morning fog, especially in winter.
Answer: Temperature inversion

quiz.q: The flow of cold, dense air down hill slopes at night into valleys is called:
quiz.explain: Cold air drains downslope like water and collects in valleys.
steps: At night cold, dense air flows downslope under gravity like water.
This is air drainage; the air collects in valleys.
Answer: Air drainage

quiz.q: Air drainage protects plants on hill slopes because:
options: Cold air collects in valley bottoms, leaving slopes warmer
Cold air rises up the slopes
quiz.explain: Frost forms in valley bottoms where cold air pools, sparing the slopes.
steps: Cold air drains down and pools in valley bottoms.
The slopes stay warmer, so plants there escape frost.
Answer: Cold air collects in valley bottoms, leaving slopes warmer
quiz.mistake: Reverses the movement of cold air

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Smoke and dust collect near the ground during a surface inversion.
Reason (R): Inversion creates stable air that does not rise easily.
options: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Stable air traps pollutants beneath the inversion layer, spreading them horizontally.
steps: A: smoke and dust collect near the ground in a surface inversion. True.
R: inversion creates stable air that does not rise easily. True.
Stable air traps pollutants below it, so R explains A.
Answer: Both A and R are true and R explains A

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'How can it be warmer higher up? Isn't that backwards?'
teach.praise: Inversion on long, clear, calm nights traps fog and smoke, and air drainage fills valleys with frost. Gappu has flipped the lapse rate!
teach.nudge: Explain inversion, its ideal conditions, its effects and air drainage.

revise.summary: In an inversion, temperature increases with height. It forms on long, clear, calm winter nights, is normal over polar areas, makes the lower air stable, and traps fog, smoke and dust. Air drainage pools cold air in valleys, leaving slopes warmer.
focus: Air drainage and frost in valleys
remember: Inversion: temperature rises with height
Ideal: long winter night, clear sky, still air; normal all year over polar areas
Air drainage: cold air flows downslope → frost in valleys, slopes warmer
traps: Inversion brings stability, not instability
Frost forms on valley floors, not on mid-slopes
